Secede

sih-SEED -- from Latin se- ('apart') + cedere ('to go, yield'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To secede is to withdraw formally, as a group or region, from membership in a larger organization, alliance, or nation.

Frustrated by the new dues structure, three chapters threatened to secede from the national club.

Worked Example

When the co-op raised membership fees for the third year running, the smallest farms banded together and voted to secede entirely.

That formal, deliberate act of pulling out of a group you used to belong to is exactly what it means to secede.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

withdraw: to formally pull out of a group

break away: to separate dramatically and completely from a larger group

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

join: to become a member of a group

unite: to come together as one

Where it sits · how final the split becomes — withdraw → secede → break away

withdraw vs. secede: Withdraw is milder than secede: a sponsor can quietly withdraw its support from a tournament, while to secede is to formally cut ties with an entire nation or alliance.

break away vs. secede: Breaking away is stronger than seceding: a region secedes through formal withdrawal, but a province that breaks away makes the fiercer, final rupture of declaring itself independent.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — se-

prefix — se-: apart, aside (Latin)

root — -cede-

root — -cede-: to go, yield (Latin (cedere))

Put it together

Put it together: Secede combines se- ('apart') with cedere ('to go, yield') -- so to secede is literally to go apart from a group you were once part of.

Use the root in a new word: proceed

Use the root in a new word: proceed: Once the paperwork was signed, the two companies were finally free to proceed with the merger.

Root Check

Word Choice

Secede is almost always used for formal, large-scale withdrawals -- a state, a province, a club chapter -- rather than one person quietly quitting something small.
